chapter.name: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
chapter.blurb: How mixtures become solutions, how much solute a fixed amount of solvent can hold, and how temperature changes that limit differently for solids and gases; then how density describes why some objects float and others sink, how it is calculated from measured mass and volume, and how temperature and pressure change it, including why ice floats on water.

Measuring mass with a balance, mass versus weight, and measuring volume with a measuring cylinder including least count and meniscus reading
Measuring the volume of regular and irregular solids and calculating density from measured mass and volume
Effect of temperature on density, including why ice floats on water

concepts.name: Solute, solvent and solution
concepts.description: What makes a mixture a solution, and the rule for telling which substance is the solute and which is the solvent.
concepts.idea: A solution is a uniform mixture in which the components are evenly distributed; when a solid dissolves in a liquid the solid is always the solute and the liquid is always the solvent, but when two liquids mix, the substance present in the smaller amount is called the solute.
concepts.rule: When sugar and salt are mixed with water, the mixture is uniform: the sweet and salty taste is the same in every sip, because the components are evenly distributed throughout. This kind of uniform mixture is called a solution. When chalk powder, sand or sawdust is mixed with water instead, the components are not evenly distributed and can be seen separately; such mixtures are called non-uniform mixtures, not solutions. Whenever a solid is mixed with a liquid to form a solution, the solid component is called the solute and the liquid component is called the solvent, no matter how much of each is present. When a solution is formed by mixing two liquids instead, it is not always clear which one is dissolving the other, so in that case the substance present in the smaller amount is called the solute and the one present in the larger amount is called the solvent.
concepts.example: The chashni (sugar syrup) of gulab jamun has a large amount of sugar dissolved in a small amount of water, yet water is still called the solvent and sugar the solute, because the solid-in-liquid rule does not depend on quantity.

concepts.name: Saturated and unsaturated solutions, concentration and solubility
concepts.description: How much solute a fixed amount of solvent can dissolve, and the terms used for solutions that can dissolve more, cannot dissolve more, or are more or less concentrated.
concepts.idea: A solution that can still dissolve more solute at a given temperature is unsaturated; once no more solute can dissolve and any extra settles at the bottom, it is saturated, and the maximum amount of solute a fixed quantity of solvent can dissolve at a temperature is its solubility.
concepts.rule: When salt is added spoon by spoon to a glass of water and stirred, it dissolves completely at first. After a few more spoons, a stage comes when the added salt no longer dissolves completely and the extra salt settles at the bottom. Before this stage, when more solute could still be dissolved at that temperature, the solution is called an unsaturated solution. Once the solute stops dissolving and starts settling, the solution is called a saturated solution at that particular temperature. The amount of solute present in a fixed quantity of solution or solvent is called its concentration. A solution with a smaller amount of solute is called a dilute solution, and one with a larger amount of solute is called a concentrated solution; dilute and concentrated are relative terms, so one solution can only be called more dilute or more concentrated compared with another. The maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a fixed quantity of solvent at a particular temperature is called its solubility.
concepts.example: A solution made with one spoon of salt in a glass of water is dilute compared with the same amount of water with three spoons of salt stirred in.

concepts.name: Effect of temperature on solubility of solids and gases
concepts.description: How raising the temperature of water changes how much of a solid can dissolve in it, and how it has the opposite effect on dissolved gases.
concepts.idea: For most solid solutes, solubility increases as temperature increases, so a saturated solution can dissolve more once heated; for gases dissolved in water, solubility generally decreases as temperature increases, which is why cold water holds more dissolved oxygen than warm water.
concepts.rule: When baking soda is added to water at 20 degrees Celsius and stirred until some remains undissolved at the bottom, the water is saturated at that temperature. Heating the same mixture to 50 degrees Celsius makes the undissolved baking soda dissolve; heating it further to 70 degrees Celsius allows even more to dissolve. This shows that for most substances, the solubility of a solid increases as temperature increases, and a solution that was saturated at a lower temperature behaves like an unsaturated solution once its temperature is raised. Gases such as oxygen also dissolve in water, forming a uniform mixture, and even in tiny amounts, this dissolved oxygen is what sustains aquatic life such as fish and plants. However, gases behave the opposite way to solids: the solubility of a gas in water generally decreases as temperature increases. This means more oxygen can dissolve in cold water than in warm water, so cold water provides more oxygen for aquatic life, while warming water reduces the oxygen dissolved in it.
concepts.example: Heating a saturated solution of baking soda in water from 20 degrees Celsius to 70 degrees Celsius lets more baking soda dissolve, but warming a pond's water reduces the amount of oxygen dissolved in it.

concepts.name: Density: meaning, formula and relative density
concepts.description: Why some objects float and others sink, how density is defined as mass per unit volume, and how relative density compares a substance's density with that of water.
concepts.idea: Density describes how much mass is packed into a given volume of a substance, given by Density = Mass / Volume; it does not depend on the shape or size of the object, though it does depend on temperature and pressure, and relative density compares a substance's density with the density of water.
concepts.rule: Some objects float in water while others sink; husk floats when washing rice while the rice itself sinks, and oil floats on water. It is generally believed that objects that float in a liquid are lighter, and those that sink are heavier, than the liquid. A wooden stick and an iron rod of the same size feel very different in weight because of a property called density, which describes the heaviness of an object. Just as a crowded bus or a forest with trees close together has high density, while a bus with only a few people or a forest with trees far apart has low density, density in science is defined as the mass present in a unit volume of a substance, given by the formula Density = Mass / Volume. Density does not depend on the shape or size of an object, but it does depend on temperature and pressure; pressure mainly affects the density of gases, and its effect on solids and liquids is negligible. The SI unit of density is kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m3), though for liquids, grams per millilitre (g/mL) or grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm3) are also commonly used, and 1 kg/m3 equals 1 gram per litre. Since 1 mL of water has a mass of close to 1 gram at room temperature, comparing a substance's density with the density of water gives its relative density, a number without units, found using Relative density = Density of the substance / Density of water at that temperature.
concepts.example: An aluminium block with a mass of 27 grams and a volume of 10 cubic centimetres has a density of 2.7 g/cm3, so its relative density with respect to water is 2.7.

concepts.name: Measuring mass and volume to calculate density
concepts.description: How mass is measured with a balance, how volume is measured with a measuring cylinder for regular and irregular objects, and how these measurements combine to calculate density.
concepts.idea: Mass is measured with a balance and volume with a measuring cylinder or the formula length times width times height for regular solids, or by water displacement for irregular solids; combining a measured mass with a measured volume gives the density using Density = Mass / Volume.
concepts.rule: Mass, the quantity of matter in an object, is measured using a balance; with a digital weighing balance, the reading is first zeroed or tared, an empty watch glass or beaker is placed on the pan and the balance is tared again, and then the object is placed on it so the display shows its mass directly, such as 16.400 g for a stone. Mass and weight are often used loosely as the same thing in everyday language, but mass is the quantity of matter in an object, measured in grams or kilograms, while weight is the force with which the Earth attracts the object, measured in newtons; most balances actually measure weight but show the result in mass units. Volume is measured using a measuring cylinder, a narrow, tall, transparent container marked with a scale; liquids form a curved surface called a meniscus, which should be read at the bottom of the meniscus for colourless liquids and at the top for coloured liquids, with the eyes level with the reading. The smallest volume a measuring cylinder can read, its least count, depends on its capacity: about 0.1 mL for a 10 or 25 mL cylinder, 1 mL for a 100 mL cylinder, 2 mL for a 250 mL cylinder and 5 mL for a 500 mL cylinder, so the cylinder whose capacity best matches the amount being measured, such as a 100 mL cylinder for 70 mL of water, gives an accurate reading in a single step. The volume of a regular solid such as a cuboid is found using Volume = length x width x height, while the volume of an irregular solid such as a stone is found by water displacement: noting the initial volume of water in a cylinder, lowering the object in, noting the final volume, and subtracting the initial volume from the final volume to get the object's volume in cm3. Once mass and volume have both been measured, density is calculated using Density = Mass / Volume.
concepts.example: A stone with a measured mass of 16.400 g that raises the water level in a measuring cylinder from 50 mL to 55 mL has a volume of 5 cm3 and a density of 16.400 divided by 5, which is 3.28 g/cm3.

concepts.name: Effect of temperature and pressure on density
concepts.description: Why heating usually lowers a substance's density and cooling raises it, the special way water behaves as it freezes into ice, and how pressure affects the density of gases, liquids and solids differently.
concepts.idea: Heating a substance generally increases its volume without changing its mass, so its density decreases, while cooling has the opposite effect; water is unusual because it expands rather than contracts as it freezes into ice, making ice less dense than liquid water and able to float; pressure mainly increases the density of gases, and has only a small or negligible effect on liquids and solids.
concepts.rule: As temperature increases, the particles of a substance, whether solid, liquid or gas, tend to move apart and spread out, so its volume increases while its mass stays the same; since Density = Mass / Volume, this means density decreases on heating and increases on cooling. This is why hot air, being less dense than the cooler air around it, rises, which is the principle a hot air balloon works on. Water behaves unusually near its freezing point: its density is highest at 4 degrees Celsius, and as it cools further and freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius, its particles rearrange into a structure that takes up more space, called expansion; because the same mass of water now occupies a larger volume, its density decreases, making ice less dense than liquid water, so ice floats. This matters for animals in lakes and oceans because the floating ice layer keeps the water underneath warm enough for fish and other creatures to survive even in very cold weather. Pressure affects density differently depending on the state of matter: for gases, increasing pressure pushes the particles closer together, decreasing volume and increasing density; for liquids, which are nearly incompressible, pressure has only a small effect; and for solids, whose particles are already very close together, changes in density caused by pressure are usually negligible.
concepts.example: When a test tube of water is heated in a beaker of hot water at about 70 degrees Celsius, the water level in a narrow glass tube fitted to it rises, because the water's volume increases as it is heated while its mass stays the same.
